vignette:
Mariana is a 37-year-old hotel manager who has been in a relationship for the past four years. She came to therapy at the urging of her partner, who had grown increasingly concerned about the changes he had witnessed in her over the last eighteen months. The trauma that had set these changes in motion occurred at a regional hospitality conference in Chicago, where she had attended an evening networking event. A colleague from another hotel chain, a man she had met briefly at previous conferences, had offered to walk her back to her hotel room. She remembered the elevator ride, remembered him asking for a glass of water at her door, and then remembered nothing—or rather, she remembered fragments that would not assemble into a story. She knew what had happened, could feel the bruise on her wrist and the soreness in her thighs the next morning, but when she tried to put the sequence into words, her mind went blank. The shame came first, before any coherent thought. When she tried to tell her partner a week later, she had wept without being able to say what had actually occurred, and she had not tried again.

In the months that followed, Mariana threw herself into her work with an intensity that her staff found commendable but her partner found alarming. She began arriving at the hotel before dawn and staying past midnight, scheduling back-to-back meetings, personally inspecting every room, rewriting the entire housekeeping protocol. She told herself she was being thorough, but what she actually feared were the quiet moments. When there was no one around, no task demanding her attention, the memory surfaced—not as a narrative but as a physical sensation: her stomach clenching, her chest tightening, her skin crawling as though she were still there. Her body kept reacting as if the danger were present, and she had come to believe that her body was not her ally. It had betrayed her during the assault, and it betrayed her now by refusing to let her feel safe.

She became unable to look at men who resembled the assailant—stocky, dark-haired men in their early forties. At the hotel, she found herself avoiding the maintenance staff, the contractors, even certain guests. She would delegate check-ins to her front desk manager whenever a guest fit that description, inventing reasons to stay in her office. This avoidance had narrowed her world considerably, and several of her colleagues had noticed that she seemed "on edge" around certain people. She did not explain why.

What consumed most of her mental energy, however, was a loop she could not escape: replaying the night of the assault and imagining what she would do if she ever saw him again. She rehearsed confrontations, imagined humiliating him in front of a crowd, fantasized about reporting him to the hotel association and destroying his career. These fantasies gave her a fleeting sense of power, but they also kept her tethered to the event, pulling her back into it dozens of times each day. She was certain that the assault had happened because of the sort of person she was—too trusting, too friendly, too eager to please. She believed there was something fundamentally wrong with her, that other women would have known better, would have fought back, would have pressed charges. She had not done any of those things. She had simply gone to work the next morning and pretended nothing had happened.

The consequences of her avoidance and overwork had accumulated quietly. Her partner had stopped asking about the conference. He had stopped trying to initiate sex, sensing her tension, and their conversations had become practical and brief. She knew he was hurt, but she could not explain to him what she could not explain to herself. What finally brought Mariana to seek help was a panic attack in the hotel lobby three weeks ago, triggered by a guest who had the same build and the same walk as the man from Chicago. She had excused herself, locked herself in a supply closet, and sat on the floor shaking for twenty minutes. Her assistant manager had found her there. The next day, her partner called a therapist and made the appointment himself. Mariana came because she did not know what else to do. She was afraid that if she kept going this way, she would lose her job, her relationship, and whatever was left of the person she used to be. She was also afraid of what it would mean to stop working, to sit still, to let the full weight of the memory catch up with her.
